Multitenant Architecture
The multitenant architecture enables an Oracle database to be a multitenant container
database (CDB).
A non-CDB is a traditional Oracle database that cannot contain PDBs. A CDB is a single
physical database that contains zero, one, or many user-created pluggable databases.
2

Manageability
Database consolidation
Cost reduction for hardware Convenient and efficient manageability
Easier and more rapid movement of data Easier upgrade of data and code by
and code unplugging and plugging in PDBs
Easier management and monitoring of the Easier testing by using PDBs for development
physical database before plugging them in to the production CDB
Separation of data and code Ability to flash back an individual PDB to a
previous SCN
Ability to set performance limits for memory
and I/O at the PDB level
Rapid provisioning and cloning using SQL
Manage many databases as one

Database Consolidation
Non CDB

Physical Architecture of a CDB in Local Undo Mode
Each PDB has got separate SYSAUX, SYSTEM and UNDO tablespaces

Challenges for a Non-CDB Architecture
• There are significant no. of databases in larger enterprises. Each DB has to be
administered separately.
• Scaling is challenging
• Server resources utilization is not optimal

A production deployment need to take place with eight Oracle

▪ Discuss solution approaches available to facilitate business requirement.

Oracle Net Services Architecture
▪ Oracle Net Services is a suite of networking components that provides
enterprise-wide connectivity solutions in distributed, heterogeneous
computing environments.
▪ Oracle Net Services enables a network session from an application to a
database instance and a database instance to another database
instance.
▪ Oracle Net Services provides location transparency, centralized
configuration and management, and quick installation and configuration

Oracle Net Listener
▪ Listener is a server-side process that
listens for incoming client connection
requests and manages traffic to the
database.
▪ The instance contacts a listener and
establishes a communication pathway to
this instance.
▪ The database services running are
registered with the listener by LREG
process
A service name is a logical representation of a database, which is the way a database is
presented to clients. A single database can be presented as multiple services.

Databases and Listeners
One listener can listen for
more than one databases
and one database can be
listened by a more than one
listeners
4

Establishing a Database Connection
After connection is
established, client
directly communicates
with server
5

Service Name
▪ A service name is a logical representation of a service
used for client connections. When a client connects
to a listener, it requests a connection to a service.
▪ When a database instance starts, it registers itself with
a listener as providing one or more services by name.
Thus, the listener acts as a mediator between the client
and instances and routes the connection request to
the right place.
▪ Multiple services can be available in a single database
6

Overview of Services in a CDB
Clients must connect to PDBs using services. A connection using a
service name starts a new session in a PDB.
7

▪ Oracle Net Configuration Assistant launched by Oracle Universal Installer

The default listener configuration file is listener.ora and it is in
$ORACLE_HOME/network/admin
An Oracle database get registers with default listener just after starting it
listener.ora file contains following parameters
▪ Name of the listener
▪ Protocol addresses that the listener is accepting connection requests on
▪ Valid nodes that the listener allows to register with the database
▪ Database services
▪ Control parameters

Question
▪ Mention steps involved to establish a client session
Answer:
1. The client initiates a connect request by providing a connect identifier.
2. The connect identifier is resolved to a connect descriptor by a naming method.
This information is returned to the client.
3. The client makes the connection request to the address provided in the connect
descriptor.
4. A listener receives the request and directs it to the appropriate database server.
5. After success verification of username and password, the connection is accepted
by the database server.

Creating & Managing User Accounts
For any user to access a database a user account is required. When user account is
available user can access the database using appropriate authentication method.
Password is the most common authentication method.
• There are many attributes related to a user account
- Username, password, default tablespace, temporary tablespace, tablespace quota and profiles
• It is mandatory to provide values for username and password when new user is created. Providing
values for other attributes is optional
• After a user account is created, except username all other attributes of a user account can be
altered
2

What is Profile ?
▪ A profile is a named set of resource limits that restrict a user's database usage and
instance resources, as well as password practices.
▪ Individual users can be allocated with different profiles
▪ At a time, each user can have only one profile.
▪ If a profile assigned to a user is dropped, that user is automatically allocated for
default profile
3

Create User
▪ Ex: Create user TEST with password test123
Assign default tablespace as ‘USERS’ and assingn10MB as the quota on the
tablespace
Specify temporary tablespace to be ‘TEMP’
Specify profile as ‘MONITORING_PROFILE’
▪ SQL > create user test identified by test123
default tablespace USERS
temporary tablespace TEMP
quota 110m on users
profile MONITORING_PROFILE;
4

Alter User
▪ Except the username all other attributes of a user can be altered.
▪ Ex:
Alter such that quota 100KB on tablespace TOOLS
Alter user’s profile to default
5

Alter User cont.
▪ SQL> alter user test
quota 100K on TOOLS
Profile DEFAULT;
▪ By default an individual user has privileges only to change their own password.
SQL> alter user test identified by test321;
▪ To change other attributes, required SYSTEM privilege should to be granted for each
user.
6

Managing Privileges
▪ While grating privileges, the principal of least privilege is followed
▪ Privileges allow a user to access database objects or execute stored programs that
are owned by another user.
▪ Privileges also enable a user to perform system-level operations, such as connecting
to the database, creating a table, or altering the database.
▪ Different categories of privileges are;
▪ Object privileges: Permissions on schema objects such as tables, views, sequences, procedures,
and packages. To use a schema object owned by another user, you need privileges on that object.
▪ System privileges: Permissions on database-level operations, such as connecting to the database,
creating users, altering the database, or consuming unlimited amounts of tablespace.
▪ Role privileges: Object and system privileges that a user has by way of a role. Roles are tools for
administering groups of privileges.
7

Granting Object Privileges
▪ Object privileges allow grantee to use schema objects own by another user in
particular way.
▪ There are different types of object privileges. Some privileges apply only to certain
types of objects.
▪ Ex:
▪ Table object privileges
SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE,DELETE etc.
▪ View object privileges
SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, REFERNCES etc.
▪ Sequence object privileges
SELECT, ALTER
▪ Stored functions, procedures, packages, and Java object privileges
DEBUG, EXECUTE
8

Granting Object Privileges - Examples
▪ Object privilege can be granted to another user or ROLE in a DB.
▪ ROLE is a collection of privileges in a DB.
▪ Ex: grant SELECT privilege on table CUSTOMER to user test.
SQL > grant SELECT on SALES.CUSTOMER to TEST;
▪ Ex: Grant SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE privileges on CUSTOMER to TEST
SQL > grant SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE on SALES.CUSTOMER to TEST;
▪ If you grant privileges to the special user PUBLIC, you make them available to all
current and future database users. For example, to give all database users the
SELECT privilege on table CUSTOMERS,
SQL > grant SELECT on SALES.CUSTOMERS to PUBLIC;
9

Granting & Revoking Object Privileges
▪ When privilege is granted WITH GRANT OPTION, grantee can grant those privileges
to other users and ROLEs
▪ Ex:
SQL> grant select on SALES.CUSTOMERS to TEST with grant option;
▪ Privileges granted can be removed with REVOKE command.
▪ Ex:
SQL> revoke SELECT on SLAES.CUSTOMER from TEST;
▪ The revoking of object privilege cascades
10

System Privileges
▪ In general, system privileges permit the grantee to execute Data Definition Language
(DDL) statements—such as CREATE, ALTER, and DROP—or Data Manipulation
Language (DML) statements system wide.
▪ Oracle 12c has more than 170 system privileges, all of which are listed in the data
dictionary view SYSTEM_PRIVILEGE_MAP.
Ex:
Job Scheduler: CREATE JOB, CREATE ANY JOB, MANAGE SCHEDULER
Indexes: CREATE ANY INDEX, ALTER ANY INDEX, DROP ANY INDEX
Procedure: CREATE PROCEDURE, EXECUTE PROCEDURE
ALTER DATABASE, ALTER SYSTEM
11

System Privileges
▪ Unlike object privileges, revocation of system privileges does not cascade.
▪ As with object privileges, you can grant system privileges to the special user PUBLIC.
Granting privileges to PUBLIC allows anyone with a database account to exercise
this privilege.
▪ Take care when system privileges are granting to PUBLIC
▪ When privilege is granted WITH ADMIN OPTION, grantee can grant those privileges to
other users and ROLEs
▪ Grantor, DBA or other privilege user can revoke the privileges granted to grantee.
▪ Ex:
▪ SQL> revoke CREATE TABLE from TEST;
▪ SQL> revoke FLASHBACK any table from public;
▪ SQL> revoke CREATE INDEX, EXCUTE ANY PROCEDURE from TEST;
12

Role Privileges
▪ A Role consists of collection of SYSTEM and OBJECT privileges. Also, one role can be granted to another role.
▪ This makes privilege management easier.
▪ Roles can be password protected.
▪ To create a role, use the CREATE ROLE statement. INDENTIFIED BY clause is optional that requires users to authenticate
themselves before enabling the role.
▪ At a time more than one role can be enabled per user.
▪ Ex:
create role APPLICATION
SQL > create ROLE APPLICATION;
grant privileges to that role
SQL > grant select any table, create any procedure to APPLICATION;
SQL > grant select on SALES.CUSTOMER to APPLICATION;
13

Setting Default Roles
▪ Roles that are enabled by default when you log on are called default roles. You do
not need to specify a password for default roles and do not have to execute a SET
ROLE statement to enable a default role.
▪ Default role for a user account can be changed with ALTER USER <user name>
DEFAULT ROLE role_list statement
14

Undo Data
▪ A copy of original, pre-modified data, stored in UNDO tablespace.
▪ Captured for every transaction that changes data.
▪ Retain at least until the transaction is ended.
▪ The amount of undo data that is retained and time for which it is retained depend on
the amount of DB activity and DB configuration.
▪ By default, Oracle database manages undo data automatically
2

Uses of Undo Data
▪ Roll back transactions: if user wants to undo the transaction before commit.
▪ Read-consistent queries: Once a query starts, any changes to the query’s underlying
tables are not reflected in the query’s results.
▪ Flashback query: Flashback query allows a user to see how a table looked at some
point in the past. As long as the undo data still exists for the requested point of
time.
▪ Database recovery: uncommitted changes in the data files are roll backed during
instance recovery after an instance crash.
▪ Recover from logical corruptions: using Oracle Flashback features.
3

Understanding Undo Segments
• Like all other segments undo segments are
made up of extents which, in turn, consists of
data blocks.
• Undo segments are automatically created by
the instance as needed to support
transactions.
• Each transaction is assigned to only one undo
segment.
• An undo segment can serve more than one
transaction at a time.

Storing Undo Information
▪ Undo information is stored in special tablespace called UNDO tablespace. If not
dedicated UNDO tablespace is created, undo data are stored in SYSTEM tablespace.
▪ At a time, a DB has ONLY ONE active undo tablespace, though DB can have more
than one UNDO tablepsaces.
▪ Undo tablespace can be recovered only while the instance in MOUNT state.
▪ Undo segments are always owned by SYS.
▪ Undo tablespaces are permanent. They are managed like any other tablespace with
the exception of recovery. Because undo is required to recover from failed
transactions.
▪ Undo tablespaces must be sized so that they can contain the original information
for all transactions.
5

Undo Data Versus Redo Data
Undo Redo
Record of How to undo a change How to do a change
again
Used for Rollback, read- Rolling forward DB
consistency change
Stored in Undo segments Redo log files
Protects against Inconsistent reads in Data loss

6

Monitoring Undo
▪ The areas to monitor include
- free space in an undo tablespace
- ‘snapshot too old errors’.
▪ Since undo information is retained until end of the transaction, for a transaction
which generates large amount of undo data requires same space on UNDO
tablespace. If not sufficient, user receives an error.
▪ Another problem may be encountered when a query needs to access undo
information that has been already overwritten.
▪ This may happen when a query needs “snapshot” of data as of some time in the
past, and the snapshot requires undo data that no longer exists.
7

Administering Undo
▪ Administrator intervention for undo management include preventing; space errors in
an undo tablespace and “snapshot too old errors”
▪ To prevent “snapshot too old” errors:
- configure an appropriate undo retention interval
- size the undo tablespace properly
- consider guaranteeing undo retention
▪ To prevent space errors in an undo tablespace:
- Size the undo tablespace properly
- Ensure that large transactions commit periodically
8

Undo Retention
▪ If there is no ‘Space Pressure ’ Oracle keeps undo data for longer period. The same
data is used by Flashback features and long running queries.
▪ The UNDO_RETENTION initialization parameter specifies (in seconds) the minimum
amount of time that Oracle database attempts to retain old undo information before
overwriting it.
▪ But, this does not guarantee that database will never overwrite undo data before
undo retention period.
▪ If no space in undo tablespae for new DML transactions, database overwrites old
undo data without keeping the time duration mention in the UNDO_RETENTION
parameter.
▪ To guarantee the retention of old undo data, undo tablespace should be created or
altered with RETENTION GUARANTEE option.
9

Categories of Undo Information
• There are three categories of undo information.
1. Uncommitted undo(current undo) information: supports a currently running
transaction, and it is required if a user wants to roll back or if the transaction has
failed. Uncommitted undo information is never overwritten.
2. Committed undo information: is no longer need to support a running transaction,
but its retention period is less than expected retention period. It is also known as
“unexpired” undo information. Committed undo information is retained when
possible by default, without causing an active transaction to fail because of lack
of space.
3. Undo data which is available for time period greater than the UNDO_RETENTION,
is called “expired undo” information. It is no longer needed to support a running
transaction. Expired undo information is overwritten when space is required by an
active transaction.
10

Sizing the Undo Tablespace
▪ Undo tablespaces must be sized so that they can contain the original information
for all transactions.
▪ It is not advisable to enable automatic extension for datafiles in undo tablespace.
11

Introduction
▪ In a multiuser database, statements with multiple simultaneous transactions can
update the same data.
▪ Transactions executing simultaneously must produce consistent results.
▪ Therefore, multiuser database system must provide data concurrency and data
consistency.
▪ Data concurrency
▪ Which ensures that users can access data at the same time
▪ Data consistency
▪ Which ensures that each user sees a consistent view of data, including visible changes made by
user’s own transactions and committed transactions of other users.
2

Locking Mechanism
▪ Designed to provide the maximum possible degree of data concurrency within the DB.
▪ Transactions that modify data acquire row-level locks rather than block-level or table-
level locks.
▪ Modifications to objects obtain object-level locks rather than schema level or DB-level.
▪ Data queries do not require a lock, and query succeeds even if someone has locked the
data.
▪ When multiple transactions need to lock same resource, queue mechanism is
established, and this is served FIFO basis. This queue mechanism is automatic, and no
administration is required.
▪ All locks are released after COMMIT or ROLLBACK command.
▪ If transaction fails, PMON releases locks held by the transaction.
3

Lock Modes
▪ Oracle Database uses two modes of locking in a multiuser database:
▪ Exclusive locks (X locks)
▪ if a transaction holds an exclusive lock on row/table then a request from some other transaction on
row/table will be denied
▪ Shared locks (S locks)
▪ if a transaction holds a shared lock on row/table then a request from other transactions for an X lock will be
denied
▪ a request from other transactions for a S lock on row/table will be granted

Locking Behavior of Readers & Writers
▪ A row is locked only when modified by a writer.
▪ A writer of a row blocks a concurrent writer of the same row.
▪ Reader never blocks a writer.
▪ The only exception is SELECT ……. FOR UPDATE statement.
▪ A writer never blocks a reader.
5

Oracle Database Locks
Locks play a crucial role in maintaining
database concurrency and consistency.
In general database uses two types of
locks: exclusive locks and share locks.
Locking is performed automatically.

▪ Deadlock arise when two or more sessions wait for data locked by each other.

Statement Failures
▪ Statement failures occur when a single database operation fails, such as a single INSERT
statement or creation of a table.
▪ Attempts to access tables without the appropriate privileges - Provide the appropriate
privileges or create views on the tables and grant privileges on the view.
▪ Running out of space - Add space to the tablespace, increase the user’s quota on the
tablespace, or enable resumable space allocation.
▪ Logic errors in applications - Work with developers to correct program errors or provide
additional logic in the application to recover gracefully from unavoidable errors
3

User Process Failures
▪ Abnormal termination of a user session is termed as a user process failure.
▪ If PMON finds a disconnected session, it rolls back the uncommitted transaction and releases
locks held by that session.
▪ Causes of user process failures are
- A user closes their SQL*Plus window without logging out.
- The workstation reboots suddenly before the application can be closed.
- The application program causes an exception and closes before the application can
be terminated normally.
- A user process times out and Oracle disconnects the session.
4

Network Failures
▪ When network component between the client and the database server fails, and the session
is disconnected from the database.
▪ In real situations, database server and your workstation are in different locations. Always
network connection is required to establish the connection between server and clients.
▪ Following scenarios can be considered as network failures.
- Listener failure
- Network connection or NIC failure

User Error Failures
▪ Though operations are succeeded from statement point of view users can still inadvertently
delete or modify data in tables or drop tables or indexes. This is known as user error failure.
▪ Also this can lead to problems of both availability issue and data corruption. Hence,
sometomes user errors can be a serious failure.

Instance Failures
▪ An instance failure occurs when the instance shuts down without synchronizing all the
database files to the same system change number (SCN) appearing the control files, requiring
a recovery operation the next time the instance is started. Many of the reasons for instance
failure are out of our control.
▪ Here are few causes of instance failures
- A power outage
- A server hardware failure
- Failure of an Oracle background process
- Emergency shutdown procedures (intentional power outage or SHUTDOWN ABORT )

▪ There are number of background processes used in instance recovery.
▪ Checkpoint (CKPT), LogWriter(LGWR), Archiver(ARCn)
▪ Instance recovery involves two distinct operations
▪ Rolling forward: data files are restored to their state before the instance failed
▪ Rolling back: changes made but not committed are returned to their original state

High Availability(HA) and Disaster Recovery(DR)
▪ HA : Ensuring continuous operational uptime with minimal service interruption.
▪ DR : Strategies and processes to restore operations after a catastrophic failure.
▪ Critical for business continuity, data integrity, and customer trust.

High Availability Concepts
• Computing environments configured to provide nearly
full-time availability are known as high availability
systems
• Note that high availability isn’t called perfect availability
or always available.
• Such systems typically have redundant hardware and
software that makes the system available despite failures.
• Well-designed high availability systems avoid having
single points-of-failure

High Availability Concepts
• When failures occur, the failover process moves
processing performed by the failed component to the
backup component
• The more transparent that failover is to users, the higher
the availability of the system.
• Hardware, software, environment and human resources
are basic redundancy factors

Disaster Recovery Concepts
• Disaster recovery (DR) involves a set of policies,
tools and procedures to enable the recovery or
continuation of vital technology infrastructure and
systems following a disruptive event.
• These disruptive events can be natural disasters
(e.g., earthquakes, floods, hurricanes), human-made
incidents (e.g., cyberattacks, data breaches, human
errors), or any other catastrophic occurrences that
can result in the loss of critical data and systems.
• The primary goal of disaster recovery is to minimize
downtime and data loss, allowing an organization to
return to normal operations as quickly as possible
after the disaster or disruption.

Disaster Recovery Terminology
Disaster recovery should indicate the key metrics of recovery point objective (RPO) and
recovery time objective (RTO)

Disaster Recovery Options
In many cases,
organizations use an
outsourced DR site instead
of maintaining their own
data center

Overview of Checkpoints
▪ Checkpoint happens from a background process called ‘checkpoint process’(CKPT)
▪ The CKPT process involves consistent database shutdowns, instance recovery and
database operations.
▪ CKPT is responsible for writing to the data file headers and control files
▪ CKPT occurs in a variety of situations
▪ Consistent database shutdown
▪ Online redo log switch
▪ Execution of ALTER SYSTEM CHECKPOINT statement
▪ Execution of ALTER DATABASE BEGIN BACKUP statement
▪ When DBW process triggers
▪ Tablespace read-only or taking it offline normal
▪ Shrinking a data file
▪ Executing ALTER TABLESPACE BEGIN BACKUP statement

Purpose of Checkpoints
▪ • Reduce the time required for recovery in case of an instance or media failure
▪ • Ensure that the database regularly writes dirty buffers in the buffer cache to disk
▪ • Ensure that the database writes all committed data to disk during a consistent
shutdown

Instance Recovery
▪ Instance recovery is applying records in the online redo log to data files to
reconstruct changes made after the most recent checkpoint.
▪ Oracle Database performs instance recovery automatically in the following
situations: •
The database opens for the first time after the failure of a single-instance
database or all instances of an Oracle RAC database. This form of instance recovery
is also called crash recovery. Oracle Database recovers the online redo threads of the
terminated instances together.
Some but not all instances of an Oracle RAC database fail. Instance recovery
is performed automatically by a remaining instance in the configuration.
▪ The SMON background process performs instance recovery, applying online redo
automatically. No user intervention is required.

Purpose of Instance Recovery
▪ Instance recovery ensures that the database is in a consistent state after an
instance failure.
▪ When a transaction is committed, log writer process (LGWR) writes both the
remaining redo entries in memory and the transaction SCN to the online redo log.
However, the database writer (DBW) process writes modified data blocks to the data
files whenever it is most efficient. For this reason, uncommitted changes may
temporarily exist in the data files while committed changes do not yet exist in the
data files.
▪ If an instance of an open database fails, either because of a SHUTDOWN ABORT
statement or abnormal termination, then the following situations can result:
▪ Data blocks committed by a transaction are not written to the data files and appear only in the
online redo log. These changes must be reapplied to the data files. •
▪ The data files contains changes that had not been committed when the instance failed. These
changes must be rolled back to ensure transactional consistency

CKPT in Instance Recovery
▪ Instance recovery uses checkpoints to determine which changes must be applied to
the data files. The checkpoint position guarantees that every committed change
with an SCN lower than the checkpoint SCN is saved to the data files.
▪ During instance recovery, the database must apply the changes that occur between
the checkpoint position and the end of the redo thread.

Phases of Instance Recovery
▪ The first phase of instance recovery is called cache recovery or rolling forward and
reapplies all changes recorded in the online redo log to the data files.
▪ These files could also contain uncommitted changes that were either saved to the
data files before the failure or were recorded in the online redo log and introduced
during cache recovery.
▪ The second phase of instance recovery is called rolling back. Oracle Database
applies undo blocks to roll back uncommitted changes in data blocks that were
written before the failure or introduced during cache recovery.
